extra.message: File upload validates only client-supplied Content-Type — no magic-byte verification

metadata.citation:
if not file.content_type or file.content_type not in ALLOWED_CONTENT_TYPES:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Unsupported file type")
metadata.proof: SOURCE: an attacker uploads a file with forged `Content-Type: image/png` while the actual bytes are a malicious script/executable. SINK: the check at line 61 only inspects `file.content_type` — a header entirely controlled by the HTTP client. There is NO magic-byte / file-signature verification of the content. The `ALLOWED_CONTENT_TYPES` set includes `text/plain`, `application/pdf`, and image types. An attacker can upload arbitrary file content (HTML with JS as `text/plain`, a `.php` file as `image/jpeg`, etc.). While the download endpoint uses Content-Disposition: attachment and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, the raw file stored on disk with arbitrary content still risks polyglot attacks, archive bombs, and other content-based exploits.

extra.message: API keys not invalidated when password is changed — keys remain valid after credential rotation

metadata.proof: SOURCE: user changes password via PUT /api/auth/me with `new_password`. SINK: line 172 deletes ALL `Session` rows for the user but does NOT deactivate or delete their `ApiKey` rows. The `_user_from_api_key` function in deps.py only checks that the key_hash matches, `is_active=True`, and the referenced User is active. After a password change (voluntary or forced by an admin), any leaked/compromised API key continues to grant full access. The same pattern exists in users.py:106-114 (admin update_user with new_password) and users.py:134 (disable_user) — only Sessions are purged, ApiKeys are untouched.

extra.message: Uploaded proof files containing PII/PHI stored unencrypted on filesystem

extra.message: Public API job-status endpoint bypasses field_worker restrictions — workers can cancel jobs via /api/v1

metadata.proof: SOURCE: a field_worker calls POST /api/v1/jobs/{job_id}/status with `{"status": "cancelled"}`. SINK: the internal `change_status` endpoint at jobs.py:266-267 explicitly rejects field_workers setting `cancelled` (`if user.role == models.UserRole.field_worker and new_status == models.JobStatus.cancelled: raise HTTPException(...)`). However the public API endpoint at public_api.py:52-59 only checks `user_can_modify_job` (which returns True for an assigned field_worker) and the generic status-transition map (JOB_STATUS_TRANSITIONS allows cancelled from unassigned, assigned, and en_route). A field_worker who cannot cancel a job through the internal `/api/jobs/{id}/status` route can trivially bypass that policy by hitting `/api/v1/jobs/{id}/status` with the same cookie or API key.

extra.message: Worker with null region_id bypasses region-mismatch check during job creation

metadata.proof: In create_job, the worker region guard at line 145 uses short-circuit evaluation: `if worker.region_id and worker.region_id != location.region_id`. When worker.region_id is None (globally available or database misconfiguration), the condition short-circuits to False and NO region validation occurs. A worker whose region_id was never set (perhaps intended for a different region) can be assigned to jobs in any region, bypassing intended regional isolation.

extra.message: Webhook HMAC secrets stored as plaintext in database

metadata.proof: The Webhook model stores the shared HMAC secret as a raw String(128) column — no hashing, no encryption at rest. In admin_misc.py line 41-48, `secret = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)` generates the value and it is inserted directly into the database. By contrast, passwords use password_hash and API keys use key_hash. Anyone with database read access can extract all webhook secrets and forge valid HMAC signatures on webhook deliveries. The secret is also returned in the API response body at creation time (admin_misc.py line 57).
